title: Solving Exponential Equations with Logs
short: Take a log of both sides to bring the exponent down.
trouble: Students divide by the base before taking logs, as if 3 · 2ˣ were 6ˣ.

blocks.html: When both sides can't be written with a common base, logarithms bring the exponent down where you can reach it. You will use the change-of-base idea and $e$.

Isolate the exponential part ($b^{\text{something}}$ alone on one side). Take $\ln$ (or $\log$) of both sides. The power rule brings the exponent down: $\ln(b^{u}) = u\ln b$. Solve the resulting linear equation; leave $\ln$ values as exact numbers.

Logs are one-to-one, so taking the log of both sides keeps the equation true and reversible. The power rule is the key move: the unknown was in an exponent, and now it multiplies a constant like $\ln 2 \approx 0.693$. After that it is ordinary algebra.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: $f(x) = 3 \cdot 2^x$ and $g(x) = 48$ meet at $x = 4$. Note that $3 \cdot 2^x$ is not $6^x$: the dashed curve $h(x) = 6^x$ is a different function.

blocks.html: Combining the coefficient with the base, as if $3 \cdot 2^x$ were $6^x$. The exponent belongs to the 2 only. Divide by 3 first: $3 \cdot 2^x = 48$ gives $2^x = 16$, so $x = 4$. ($6^x = 48$ would give about $2.16$, a wrong answer.) Check by substituting: $3 \cdot 2^4 = 48$.
